slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** who do not have a manager assigned.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: In SQL, `NULL` represents a **missing or unknown value**. You cannot use `=` to compare NULLs; you must use `IS NULL` to check for empty fields.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 32
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** who have a manager assigned.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `IS NOT NULL` condition filters out missing values, returning only rows where the specified column **has an actual value** stored in it.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 33
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 ORDER BY salary DESC;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** earning more than 50,000 and sort them from **highest** **salary** to **lowest**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 34
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Count the **total** number of **employees**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `COUNT(*)` function counts the **total number of rows** returned by the query, including rows that contain `NULL` or duplicate values.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 35
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT COUNT(department) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Count how many **department** values exist (ignoring **NULL** values).

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: Unlike `COUNT(*)`, passing a specific column name (like `COUNT(department)`) only counts rows where that column is **not NULL**. Missing values are ignored.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 36
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT department) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Count how many different **departments** exist.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 37
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Add up all employee **salaries** and show the **total**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `SUM()` function calculates the **total combined value** of a numeric column. It ignores any `NULL` values during the calculation.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 38
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Find the **average** **salary** of all **employees**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `AVG()` function calculates the **average value** of a numeric column. It automatically ignores `NULL` values (which means they aren't included in the sum or count).

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 39
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT MIN(salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Find the **lowest** **salary** among all **employees**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `MIN()` function scans the column to find the **smallest value** (lowest number, earliest date, or first alphabetical text) in that column.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 40
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Find the **highest** **salary** among all **employees**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `MAX()` function scans the column to find the **largest value** (highest number, latest date, or last alphabetical text) in that column.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 41
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT MAX(salary)-MIN(salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Find the difference between the **highest** and **lowest** **salary**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 42
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE department='IT';**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Count how many **employees** belong to the IT **department**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 43
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department='IT';**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Find the **average** **salary** of **employees** in the IT **department**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 44
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees WHERE department='IT';**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Find the **total** **salary** paid to **employees** in the IT **department**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 45
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT MIN(salary),MAX(salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show both the **lowest** and **highest** **salary** in the company.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 46
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_employees FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Count all **employees** and display the result with the label total_employees.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 47
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: SELECT **department**,AVG(**salary**) FROM **employees** GROUP BY **department**;

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `GROUP BY` clause collapses rows with the same value into summary rows. It is essential when you want to run aggregate functions (like count, sum, or average) for **each category**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 48
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: For each **department**, calculate the **average** **salary**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 49
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,SUM(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: For each **department**, calculate the **total** **salary** paid.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 50
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,MAX(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: For each **department**, find the **highest** **salary**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 51
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,MIN(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: For each **department**, find the **lowest** **salary**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 52
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*)>5;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show only **departments** that have more than 5 **employees**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `HAVING` clause filters **grouped summary rows** after `GROUP BY` runs. While `WHERE` filters individual rows *before* grouping, `HAVING` filters the *groups* themselves.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 53
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING AVG(salary)>60000;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show only **departments** whose **average** **salary** is greater than 60,000.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 54
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,SUM(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING SUM(salary)>500000;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show only **departments** whose **total** **salary** exceeds 500,000.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 55
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary>50000 GROUP BY department;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: For each **department**, count **employees** whose **salary** is above 50,000.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 56
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department<>'HR' GROUP BY department;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: For each **department** except HR, calculate the **average** **salary**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 57
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,COUNT(*) AS total_employees FROM employees GROUP BY department;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Count **employees** in each **department** and label the count as total_employees.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 58
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **departments** **sorted** from the largest **department** to the smallest.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 59
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department ORDER BY AVG(salary) DESC;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **departments** **sorted** from **highest** **average** **salary** to **lowest** **average** **salary**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 60
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) BETWEEN 5 AND 20;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **departments** that have between 5 and 20 **employees**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 61
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department,MAX(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING MAX(salary)>100000;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **departments** where at least one employee earns more than 100,000.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 62
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees INNER JOIN departments ON employees.department_id=departments.department_id;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** only when a matching **department** exists.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: An `INNER JOIN` matches rows between tables **only if** the join condition is met in both tables. Rows that don't have matching values are completely excluded from the results.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 63
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,department_name FROM employees INNER JOIN departments ON employees.department_id=departments.department_id;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show each employee along with their **department** **name**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 64
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees LEFT JOIN departments ON employees.department_id=departments.department_id;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show all **employees**, even if they are not assigned to any **department**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `LEFT JOIN` returns **all rows** from the left table, plus any matching rows from the right table. If there is no match on the right, it fills the missing columns with `NULL`.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 65
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees RIGHT JOIN departments ON employees.department_id=departments.department_id;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show all **departments**, even if no employee belongs to them.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `RIGHT JOIN` returns **all rows** from the right table, plus any matching rows from the left table. If there is no match on the left, it fills the missing columns with `NULL`.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 66
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees FULL OUTER JOIN departments ON employees.department_id=departments.department_id;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **everything** from both tables, whether a match exists or not.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `FULL OUTER JOIN` combines the results of both LEFT and RIGHT joins. It returns **all rows** from both tables, pairing them up where possible and filling with `NULL` where there is no match.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 67
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,department_name FROM employees LEFT JOIN departments ON employees.department_id=departments.department_id;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show every employee and their **department** **name** if one exists.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 68
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees LEFT JOIN departments ON employees.department_id=departments.department_id WHERE departments.department_id IS NULL;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** who are not assigned to any **department**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: This pattern (sometimes called an **anti-join**) is used to find rows in the left table that **do not exist** in the right table by filtering for `NULL` on the joined column.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 69
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees RIGHT JOIN departments ON employees.department_id=departments.department_id WHERE employees.emp_id IS NULL;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **departments** that currently have no **employees**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 70
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT e.name,d.department_name FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id=d.department_id;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show employee **names** and **department** **names** using shorter table **names**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 71
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department_name,COUNT(*) FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id=d.department_id GROUP BY department_name;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Count how many **employees** belong to each **department**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 72
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,department_name FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id=d.department_id WHERE department_name='IT';**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** who work in the IT **department**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 73
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,department_name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id=d.department_id ORDER BY department_name;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show all **employees** and sort them by **department** **name**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 74
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT e1.name,e2.name FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id=e2.emp_id;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** along with their managers.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A **Self Join** is a regular join where a table is joined with **itself**. You must use different table aliases (like `e1` and `e2`) so the database can tell them apart.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 75
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees CROSS JOIN departments;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Match every employee with every **department** possible.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `CROSS JOIN` creates a **Cartesian product**, pairing every single row of the first table with every single row of the second table. This can generate **massive datasets** very quickly.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 76
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department_name,AVG(salary) FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id=d.department_id GROUP BY department_name;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Calculate the **average** **salary** for each **department**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 77
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary>(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** whose **salary** is higher than the company's **average** **salary**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A **Subquery** is a query nested inside another query. A scalar subquery returns a **single value** (like the average salary) which can be used in comparison filters.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 78
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary=(SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show the employee(s) earning the **highest** **salary**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 79
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary=(SELECT MIN(salary) FROM employees);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show the employee(s) earning the **lowest** **salary**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 80
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM departments WHERE department_name='IT');**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** who work in the IT **department**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: When a subquery returns a **list of values**, you combine it with the `IN` operator. This allows the outer query to match against any value in the subquery's result list.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 81
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department_name FROM departments WHERE department_id IN (SELECT department_id FROM employees);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **departments** that have at least one employee.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 82
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT department_name FROM departments WHERE department_id NOT IN (SELECT department_id FROM employees);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **departments** that currently have no **employees**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: Using `NOT IN` with a subquery returns values that aren't in the list. **Warning:** If the subquery returns even a single `NULL` value, the entire `NOT IN` query will return **zero results**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 83
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM departments WHERE employees.department_id=departments.department_id);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** whose **department** actually exists.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `EXISTS` operator checks for the **presence of rows** returned by a subquery. It stops scanning as soon as it finds a single match, making it highly efficient for existence checks.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 84
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM departments WHERE employees.department_id=departments.department_id);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** whose **department** does not exist.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `NOT EXISTS` operator returns rows only if the subquery returns **no results**. It is a very safe and fast way to find non-matching records, even when columns contain `NULL` values.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 85
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,salary FROM employees WHERE salary>(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department_id=employees.department_id);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** earning more than the **average** **salary** of their own **department**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A **Correlated Subquery** references a column from the outer query (here, `employees.department_id`). It is evaluated **once for each row** processed by the outer query.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 86
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE department_id=(SELECT department_id FROM departments WHERE department_name='Finance');**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** who belong to the Finance **department**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 87
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary IN (SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE department_id=1);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** whose **salary** matches the **salary** of someone in **department** 1.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 88
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary>(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department_id=1);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** earning more than the **average** **salary** of **department** 1.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 89
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT city FROM customers UNION SELECT city FROM suppliers;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show all cities from both tables, removing duplicates.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `UNION` operator combines the results of two queries into one list. It automatically **removes duplicates** and sorts the results, which adds sorting overhead.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 90
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT city FROM suppliers;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show all cities from both tables, including duplicates.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: Unlike `UNION`, `UNION ALL` combines results **without removing duplicates**. Because it skips the sorting and deduplication step, it is **much faster**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 91
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT city FROM customers INTERSECT SELECT city FROM suppliers;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show cities that appear in both **customers** and suppliers tables.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `INTERSECT` operator returns only the rows that are **common** to the results of both queries. Any duplicate rows are removed from the final output.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 92
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT city FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT city FROM suppliers;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show cities that have **customers** but no suppliers.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `EXCEPT` operator (or `MINUS` in some databases) returns rows from the first query that **do not appear** in the second query's results.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 93
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT city FROM suppliers EXCEPT SELECT city FROM customers;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show cities that have suppliers but no **customers**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 94
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE department_id=1 UNION SELECT name FROM employees WHERE department_id=2;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** from **department** 1 and **department** 2 without repeating **names**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 95
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name FROM employees WHERE department_id=1 UNION ALL SELECT name FROM employees WHERE department_id=2;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **employees** from **department** 1 and **department** 2, including repeated **names** if any.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 96
revisionCards.explanation: **INSERT INTO employees(name,salary) VALUES('John',50000);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Add a new employee named John with a **salary** of 50,000.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `INSERT INTO` command adds **new rows** to a table. You specify the columns you want to fill, followed by the corresponding values.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 97
revisionCards.explanation: **INSERT INTO employees(name,department_id,salary) VALUES('Alice',2,60000);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Add a new employee named Alice to **department** 2 with a **salary** of 60,000.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 98
revisionCards.explanation: **UPDATE employees SET salary=60000 WHERE emp_id=1;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Change the **salary** of employee 1 to 60,000.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `UPDATE` command modifies existing rows. It is critical to include a `WHERE` clause so you only update the **intended rows** instead of every row in the table.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 99
revisionCards.explanation: **UPDATE employees SET department_id=3 WHERE emp_id=1;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Move employee 1 to **department** 3.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 100
revisionCards.explanation: **UPDATE employees SET salary=salary+5000;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Increase everyone's **salary** by 5,000.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: Omitting the `WHERE` clause in an `UPDATE` statement will apply the change to **every single row** in the table. Use this with caution!

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 101
revisionCards.explanation: **DELETE FROM employees WHERE emp_id=1;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Remove employee 1 from the table.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `DELETE FROM` command removes rows from a table. Always use a `WHERE` clause to target **specific records**, otherwise you will delete all data in the table.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 102
revisionCards.explanation: **DELETE FROM employees WHERE department_id=3;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Remove all **employees** who belong to **department** 3.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 103
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE TABLE employees(emp_id INT,name VARCHAR(50));**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a new **employees** table with employee ID and **name** columns.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `CREATE TABLE` command defines a new table structure. You must specify the table name, column names, and their **data types** (like `INT` or `VARCHAR`).

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 104
revisionCards.explanation: **ALTER TABLE employees ADD salary INT;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Add a new **salary** column to the **employees** table.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `ALTER TABLE ADD` command adds a **new column** to an existing table schema. On very large tables, adding columns can lock the table and cause temporary downtime.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 105
revisionCards.explanation: **ALTER TABLE employees DROP COLUMN salary;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Remove the **salary** column from the **employees** table.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN` command **permanently deletes** a column and all of its stored data. This action is irreversible!

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 106
revisionCards.explanation: **DROP TABLE employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Delete the **employees** table completely from the database.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `DROP TABLE` command completely **deletes the table structure** and all its data from the database. It is a permanent and non-reversible operation.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 107
revisionCards.explanation: **TRUNCATE TABLE employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Remove all data from the **employees** table but keep the table structure.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `TRUNCATE TABLE` command quickly **deletes all rows** from a table, but keeps the table structure intact. It is much faster than `DELETE` because it bypasses logging individual row deletions.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 108
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE TABLE employees(email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a table where no two **employees** can have the same email address.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `UNIQUE` constraint ensures that all values in a column are **distinct** from one another. It automatically generates a unique index behind the scenes for fast lookups.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 109
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE TABLE employees(emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,name VARCHAR(50));**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a table where each employee must have a **unique** ID.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `PRIMARY KEY` uniquely identifies each row in a table. It must contain **unique, non-NULL** values. A table can have only one primary key.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 110
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE TABLE employees(name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a table where every employee must have a **name**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `NOT NULL` constraint prevents a column from storing `NULL` (empty or missing) values, forcing the application to **always supply a value**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 111
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE TABLE employees(age INT CHECK(age>=18));**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Allow only **employees** who are at least 18 years old.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `CHECK` constraint enforces **business rules** at the database level by rejecting any rows where the column value makes the specified expression false.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 112
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE TABLE employees(city VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'Delhi');**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: If no city is provided, automatically set it to Delhi.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `DEFAULT` constraint specifies a **fallback value** that the database will automatically insert if no value is explicitly provided for that column.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 114
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE TABLE employees(department_id INT,FOREIGN KEY(department_id) REFERENCES departments(department_id));**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Allow **employees** to be linked only to valid **departments**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `FOREIGN KEY` links a column to the primary key of another table. It enforces **referential integrity**, ensuring you can't insert a reference to a parent row that doesn't exist.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 115
revisionCards.explanation: **ALTER TABLE employees MODIFY salary BIGINT;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Change the **salary** column's data type to hold larger values.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `ALTER TABLE MODIFY` (or `ALTER COLUMN` depending on the SQL dialect) changes a column's **data type**. Changing data types can take a long time on large tables as the database converts all existing data.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 116
revisionCards.explanation: **ALTER TABLE employees RENAME COLUMN name TO employee_name;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Change the column **name** from **name** to **employee_name**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: Renaming a column changes its name in the database schema. Be careful: any queries, backend code, or application code referencing the old column name **will break** until updated.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 117
revisionCards.explanation: **ALTER TABLE employees RENAME TO staff;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Rename the **employees** table to staff.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: Renaming a table updates its name in the database schema. Ensure that all database references and applications are updated to avoid **connection errors**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 118
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE TABLE employees(emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a table where each employee has a **unique** ID, a mandatory **name**, and a **unique** email address.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 120
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE VIEW employee_details AS SELECT name,salary FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a virtual table that shows employee **names** and **salaries**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A **View** is a saved SQL query that you can query as if it were a physical table. It acts as a **virtual table**, running the underlying query dynamically each time it is accessed.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 121
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM employee_details;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: **View** the data stored in the employee_details **view**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: Querying a view is identical to querying a normal table. However, since views run their underlying query on the fly, joining views or querying complex views can sometimes **slow down performance**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 122
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE VIEW it_employees AS SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department_id=1;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a **view** that always shows **employees** from **department** 1.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 123
revisionCards.explanation: **DROP VIEW employee_details;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Delete the employee_details **view**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `DROP VIEW` command deletes a virtual view. Dropping a view **does not delete or affect** the underlying table data.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 124
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE INDEX idx_name ON employees(name);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a shortcut on the **name** column to speed up searches.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: An **Index** is a data structure (usually a B-Tree) that helps the database find rows in a fraction of the time. While indexes speed up reads (`SELECT`), they **slow down writes** (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) because the index must be updated too.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 125
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_email ON employees(email);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a shortcut on email and make sure duplicate emails are not allowed.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A **Unique Index** serves two purposes: it accelerates queries on that column, and it **prevents duplicate values** from being inserted into the column, throwing an error if a duplicate is found.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 126
revisionCards.explanation: **CREATE INDEX idx_dept_salary ON employees(department_id,salary);**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a shortcut using both **department** and **salary** to speed up related searches.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A **Composite Index** is an index built on multiple columns. It works best when your queries filter by the columns in the **exact order** defined in the index (left-to-right).

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 127
revisionCards.explanation: **DROP INDEX idx_name;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Remove the shortcut created on the **name** column.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `DROP INDEX` command removes an index. You should drop unused indexes to save storage space and **improve write performance** on tables.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 128
revisionCards.explanation: **START TRANSACTION;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Begin a **transaction** so multiple changes can be treated as one unit.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A transaction groups multiple SQL commands into a single unit of work. Changes made during a transaction are **invisible to other users** until they are committed.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 129
revisionCards.explanation: **ROLLBACK;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Undo all changes made during the current **transaction**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `ROLLBACK` command discards all database modifications made during the active transaction, acting as a clean **undo operation**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 130
revisionCards.explanation: **SAVEPOINT sp1;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a **checkpoint** named sp1 that you can return to later.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A `SAVEPOINT` acts as a **checkpoint** inside a transaction, allowing you to rollback specific parts of your changes without undoing the entire transaction.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 131
revisionCards.explanation: **ROLLBACK TO sp1;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Undo changes made after the **checkpoint** sp1 while keeping earlier changes.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` command rolls back the transaction specifically to the checkpoint, allowing you to recover from a partial error and **continue the transaction**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 132
revisionCards.explanation: **START TRANSACTION; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-1000 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+1000 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Transfer 1,000 from account 1 to account 2 and save both changes together.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `COMMIT` command permanently saves all transaction changes to the database. Once committed, the changes are **permanent** and cannot be rolled back.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 133
revisionCards.explanation: **START TRANSACTION; DELETE FROM employees WHERE emp_id=5; ROLLBACK;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Delete employee 5, then cancel the deletion and restore the data.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 134
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,CASE WHEN salary>50000 THEN 'High' ELSE 'Low' END FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Label each employee as High or Low based on their **salary**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `CASE` statement acts like an **if-else conditional** in SQL. It evaluates conditions in order and returns the value specified in the first matching `THEN` branch.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 135
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,CASE WHEN salary>=100000 THEN 'Senior' WHEN salary>=50000 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Junior' END FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Categorize **employees** into Senior, Mid, or Junior based on **salary**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 136
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT COALESCE(phone,'No Phone') FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show the phone number, and if it's missing, show 'No Phone' instead.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `COALESCE()` function returns the **first non-NULL value** in its list of arguments. It is commonly used to supply fallback values for missing data.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 137
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT NULLIF(salary,0) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show **salary**, but convert 0 into **NULL**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `NULLIF()` function compares two arguments and returns `NULL` if they are **equal**. This is extremely useful for preventing **division-by-zero errors** in aggregates.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 138
revisionCards.explanation: **WITH high_salary AS (SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary>50000) SELECT * FROM high_salary;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a temporary result containing high-**salary** **employees** and query it.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A **Common Table Expression (CTE)** defines a temporary result set that you can reference like a table within a single query. It is a cleaner, more readable alternative to **subqueries**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 139
revisionCards.explanation: **WITH dept_avg AS (SELECT department_id,AVG(salary) avg_sal FROM employees GROUP BY department_id) SELECT * FROM dept_avg;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Create a temporary table showing the **average** **salary** of each **department**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 140
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,salary,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Give every employee a **unique** ranking number based on **salary**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `ROW_NUMBER()` window function assigns a **sequential, unique integer** starting from 1 to each row in the query result, based on the specified order.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 141
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,salary,RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Rank **employees** by **salary**, giving equal **salaries** the same rank and skipping ranks afterward.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `RANK()` window function assigns rankings. If rows have the **same value**, they get the same rank. However, it **skips ranks** for subsequent items (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 4).

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 142
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,salary,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Rank **employees** by **salary**, giving equal **salaries** the same rank without skipping ranks.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: Unlike `RANK()`, `DENSE_RANK()` does **not skip rank numbers** when duplicates exist. It returns consecutive rankings (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 3).

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 143
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,salary,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Rank **employees** within each **department** separately.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `PARTITION BY` clause divides the result set into **independent groups** (like departments) before applying the window function. The row numbering resets to 1 for each partition.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 144
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,salary,LAG(salary) OVER(ORDER BY salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show each employee's **salary** along with the previous employee's **salary**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `LAG()` window function allows you to access a value from a **previous row** in the query result. This is highly useful for calculating period-over-period growth or changes.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 145
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,salary,LEAD(salary) OVER(ORDER BY salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show each employee's **salary** along with the next employee's **salary**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `LEAD()` window function allows you to access a value from a **subsequent row** in the query result without using complex self-joins.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 146
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT salary,SUM(salary) OVER(ORDER BY salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Calculate a running **total** of **salaries**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: Combining `SUM()` with `OVER(ORDER BY ...)` calculates a **running total**. The database adds the current row's value to the sum of all preceding rows' values.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 147
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,salary,AVG(salary) OVER() FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show each employee along with the company-wide **average** **salary**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: An empty `OVER()` clause performs calculations across the **entire result set**. Here, it computes the global average salary and appends it to **every single row** without collapsing them.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 148
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT * FROM (SELECT name,salary,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) rn FROM employees) t WHERE rn<=3;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show the top 3 **highest**-paid **employees**.

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 149
revisionCards.explanation: **WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (SELECT 1 n UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM nums WHERE n<5) SELECT * FROM nums;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Generate numbers from 1 to 5 using a recursive query.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: A **Recursive CTE** references itself, executing in a loop until a termination condition is met. It is commonly used to generate sequences or traverse hierarchical data (like org charts).

revisionCards.title: SQL Statement 150
revisionCards.explanation: **SELECT name,salary,PERCENT_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary) FROM employees;**

slides.headline: 💡 Meaning
slides.body: Show where each employee stands relative to others based on **salary**.

slides.headline: 💡 Usage Details
slides.body: The `PERCENT_RANK()` function calculates the **relative rank of a row** as a percentage between 0 and 1. This is ideal for finding percentiles (e.g. who is in the top 10%).

revisionCards.title: The Art of Structured Thinking
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of International flights taking off from India per day.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Since international air traffic is not evenly distributed across airports, we categorize airports into high-, medium-, and low-traffic groups and estimate flights for each category separately.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
Before proceeding, it is important to define the scope of the problem:
1. Consider only passenger flights.
2. Include both direct and connecting international departures originating from India.
3. Exclude cargo and military flights.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition
slides.body:
**Intuition: Segmentation**:
TNot all airports contribute equally to international air traffic. Therefore, we segment airports based on traffic volume and estimate each segment separately.

⚠️ **Approach**: Classify airports into three tiers based on their level of international traffic.
Then estimate the number of flights this way:
`Total Flights = (Tier 1  Airports × Flights per Airport) + (Tier 2 Airports × Flights per Airport) + (Tier 3 Airports × Flights per Airport).`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Number of Airports**:
Assuming total number of International airports in india : `30`

 **Categorization**:
We assume that there are `8 Tier 1 airports`, `15 Tier 2 airports`, and `7 Tier 3 airports`. Tier 1 airports represent major hubs with high international traffic, Tier 2 airports handle moderate traffic, while Tier 3 airports account for relatively lower international activity.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Tier 1 Airports**:
Peak Hours: `16 × 4 flights/hour = 64 flights`
Non-Peak Hours: `8 × 2 flights/hour = 16 flights`
Flights per Airport: `80 flights`
Total number of flights: `8 × 80 = 640 flights`

**Tier 2 Airports**:
Peak Hours: `10 × 4 flights/hour = 40 flights`
Non-Peak Hours: `8 × 2 flights/hour = 16 flights`
Flights per Airport: `56 flights`
Total number of flights: `15 × 56 = 840 flights`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Tier 3 Airports**:
Peak Hours: `5 × 4 flights/hour = 20 flights`
Non-Peak Hours: `8 × 2 flights/hour = 16 flights`
Flights per Airport: `36 flights`
Total number of flights: `7 × 36 = 252 flights`

**Final Aggregation**:
Total Flights = `640 + 840 + 252 = 1732` international flights/day

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps: **Total Flights**: Thus, the total number of international flights taking off from India is **1732 flights.**

**Adjustment Factors**: Assume that around `2%` of flights get cancelled due to weather conditions, runway congestion, or aircraft malfunction. Also consider a `5%` variation in air traffic due to seasonal fluctuations.

**Final Answer**: `(1732 × 0.98) × [0.95, 1.05] = [1613, 1783]`
≈ **1700** international flights per day

revisionCards.title: Google Queries per Second
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of queries answered by Google per second.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine Google queries as questions in a huge classroom. Different age groups ask different amounts, so we estimate each group’s daily questions and convert the total into questions per second.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We are estimating only Google queries in India.
2. International searches are ignored.
3. Queries from YouTube and Google News are excluded, while Google Maps can be treated separately as an add-on.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Categorization**:
The core idea is to avoid guessing one huge number directly. Instead of guessing total queries directly, we divide India’s population into age groups and estimate Google usage for each group through phones, computers, Gemini, and voice search. Then we add all daily queries and convert the total into queries per second.
`Queries/day = Population × Internet access % × Usage share × Avg. searches/day`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Population on an average:**:
We assume India’s population to be around `150 crore`, out of which nearly `60%` have internet access. Since Google usage is not the same for everyone, we divide users into age groups. We also assume that people search through different modes like phones, computers, Gemini, and voice search, and the average number of searches depends on the age group.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Base Population**:
India’s population ≈ `150 crore`
Internet access ≈ `60%`

**Step 2: 0–14 years**:
Population share = `20%`
Active usage share = `40%`
Average searches = `2 computer searches + 4 Gemini prompts and negligible smartphone and voice assistant usage`
Calculation: `150 × 0.6 × 0.2 × 0.4 × (2 + 4) = 43.2 Cr/day`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: 14–18 years**:
Population share = `15%`
Smartphone usage share = `80%`
Computer/laptop usage share = `70%`
Tablet usage share = `25%`
Gemini usage share = `70%`
Average searches = `10 smartphone searches + 3 computer searches + 2 tablet searches + 5 Gemini prompts + 2 voice assistant searches`
Calculation: `150 × 0.6 × 0.15 ×(0.8×10 + 0.7×3 + 0.7×0.25×2 + 0.7×5 + 2) = 215.4 Cr/day`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 4: 18–50 years**:
Population share = `50%`
Smartphone usage share = `100%`
Computer/laptop usage share = `90%`
Gemini usage share = `80%`
Average searches = `15 smartphone searches + 20 computer searches + 20 Gemini prompts + 2 voice assistant searches`
Calculation: `150 × 0.5 × 0.6 × (15 + 0.9×20 + 0.8×20 + 2) = 2295 Cr/day`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Google Maps usage**: Assume `5%` of the population uses Maps frequently for travel, delivery, field work, and client visits, averaging `5 searches/day`. Also, `2 Cr` tourists/year use Maps for navigation, hotels, and local travel, averaging `5 searches/day`.
Calculation: `(Professionals)150 × 0.05 × 5 + (Tourists)2 × 5 ÷ 365 = 37.527 Cr/day`

**Final Answer**:
`Total Queries Per Day: 43.2 + 215.4 + 2295 + 37.53 = 2591.13 Cr/day`
≈ **30 lakh** google queries per second.

revisionCards.title: Declining Revenue of a Board Game Manufacturer
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A board game manufacturer in Delhi has experienced a decline in revenue over the past year. The decline is industry-wide, and revenue from Ludo has been affected the most.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Simplified Analogy**:

•Imagine a restaurant losing customers. The problem could be due to fewer visitors, changing customer preferences, stronger competitors, or alternative dining options. Similarly, we need to identify what is causing the decline in demand for board games.
•Revenue is like a machine with two key components: Supply and Demand.
•If the machine stops producing enough products, the issue lies on the supply side. If customers stop buying the products, the issue lies on the demand side.
•Our goal is to identify which side is responsible for the decline in revenue.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition
slides.body:
**Intuition: Demand-Side Analysis**:
Revenue decline can occur due to supply-side or demand-side factors.
Since competitors are facing a similar problem and the industry's supply side has remained unchanged, we can focus our analysis on demand.
To understand demand, we will examine four key drivers:
• Product
• Price
• Place
• Promotion.

slides.headline: ⚠️ The Trap vs The Clean Way
slides.body:
❌ **Common Trap**:
Assuming the decline is caused by poor product quality or manufacturing issues without validating the facts.

✅ **Preferred Approach**:
First determine whether the issue is company-specific or industry-wide. Then eliminate supply-side causes and systematically analyze demand drivers to identify the root cause.

slides.headline: 🔎 Investigating Demand
slides.body:
**Product**:
• Has product quality changed?
• Have customers shifted to substitutes?
• Are complementary items missing?

revisionCards.title: Even, Odd, Positive and Negative
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Given an array of N integers, count and print the total number of even, odd, positive, and negative values. Note that zero is considered an even number but is neither positive nor negative.
Constraints: 1<=N<=10^3 and -10^5 <=X_i <=10^5.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Idea
slides.body:
Iterate through the array of N elements and maintain **four separate counters** initialized to 0. For each element X_i, check its parity using X_i % 2 == 0 to increment the **even** or **odd** counter.

Simultaneously, check its sign where X_i > 0 increments **positive** and X_i < 0 increments **negative** (ignoring zero).

slides.headline: Code: C++ Implementation
Code: Python Implementation
slides.code:
import sys

def main():
    # Fast I/O
    input = sys.stdin.read
    data = input().split()
    
    if not data:
        return

    n = int(data[0])
    numbers = [int(x) for x in data[1:n+1]]

    even_count = 0
    odd_count = 0
    pos_count = 0
    neg_count = 0

    for x in numbers:
        # Check even or odd
        if x % 2 == 0:
            even_count += 1
        else:
            odd_count += 1

        # Check positive or negative
        if x > 0:
            pos_count += 1
        elif x < 0:
            neg_count += 1

    print(f"Even: {even_count}")
    print(f"Odd: {odd_count}")
    print(f"Positive: {pos_count}")
    print(f"Negative: {neg_count}")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Zero Behavior**: The number 0 must be counted as **even**, but it should be excluded from both the **positive** and **negative** counts.
**Independent Classifications**: Each number in the input must be evaluated for two completely separate properties: its parity (even vs. odd) and its sign (positive vs. negative).
**Constraint Boundaries**: The input array size N is small (1<=N <=10^3), but individual elements X_i can be negative, meaning your parity logic must correctly handle negative odd numbers.

revisionCards.title: GCD
revisionCards.explanation:
Problem Statement:
Given two positive integers A and B, compute and print their Greatest Common Divisor (GCD), which is the largest positive integer that divides both numbers without leaving a remainder. Constraints: 1<=A, B<=10^3.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Idea
slides.body: The most efficient way to find the GCD of two numbers is the Euclidean Algorithm. It relies on the principle that the greatest common divisor of two numbers also divides their difference, meaning gcd(A, B) = gcd(B, A mod B) until the remainder becomes 0.

slides.headline: Code: C++ Implementation
Code: Python Implementation
slides.code:
import sys
from sys import stdin, stdout

def main():
    data = stdin.read().split()
    idx = 0
    a = int(data[idx])
    idx += 1
    b = int(data[idx])
    idx += 1

    if a < b:
        a, b = b, a

    while b != 0:
        temp = b
        b = a % b
        a = temp

    stdout.write(str(a) + '
')

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Efficient Approach**: Euclidean Algorithm finds the GCD in **O(log(min(A, B)))** time, much faster than checking all divisors up to min(A, B).
**Built-in func**: Use `std::gcd()` in C++ or `math.gcd()` in Python for an optimized solution.
**Input Order Doesn't Matter**: The algorithm works correctly even if `A < B`; it automatically adjusts during the first iteration.

revisionCards.title: Digits
revisionCards.explanation:
Problem Statement:
Given a number N, print its individual digits from right to left, separated by a space. The input consists of T test cases.

Constraints: T is between 1 and 10; N is between 0 and 10^9.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Idea
slides.body:
To extract the digits from right to left, we can look at the number as a string and simply reverse it.
 Alternatively, using math, we can repeatedly take the remainder of the number divided by 10 (N % 10) to get the last digit, print it, and then divide the number by 10 (N / 10) to remove that digit.
We repeat this loop until the number becomes 0, ensuring we handle the special case where N is exactly 0.

slides.headline: Code: C++ Implementation
Code: Python Implementation
slides.code:
import sys

def main():
    input = sys.stdin.read
    data = input().split()
    
    if not data:
        return

    t = int(data[0])
    
    # Process each test case string directly
    for i in range(1, t + 1):
        s = data[i]
        # Reverse the string and join characters with a space
        reversed_digits = s[::-1]
        print(" ".join(reversed_digits))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **String Traversal**: Reversing the number as a string directly processes digits from right to left, avoiding manual digit extraction.
**Trailing Zeros**: Values like 1200 correctly become 0021, preserving all digits during reversal.
**Zero Case**: Using a string naturally handles N = 0, whereas a while (N > 0) loop would not execute.

revisionCards.title: Lucky Numbers

Constraints: A and B are between 1 and 10^5.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Idea
slides.body:
Since the upper limit of the range is relatively small (B <= 10^5), we can iterate through every integer from A to B. For each number, we check its digits either by converting it into a string or by using math (repeated modulo 10).
If we find any digit other than 4 or 7, that number is disqualified. We keep track of whether we have found at least one valid lucky number; if the loop finishes and our tracker is empty, we print -1.

slides.headline: Code: C++ Implementation
Code: Python Implementation
🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Track Results**: Use a flag to check whether any lucky number was found; print -1 if none exist.
**Early Exit**: While checking a number, stop immediately when a digit other than 4 or 7 is encountered.
**Scalable Approach**: For large ranges, generate lucky numbers directly (using recursion/BFS) instead of iterating through every number.

slides.body:

3. Revenue from OTT, online streaming rights, and non-theatre businesses is ignored.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Categorization**:
Instead of directly guessing PVR’s total revenue, we break it into smaller earning sources. First, we estimate the number of PVR screens in India, then calculate revenue from tickets, food outlets, and advertisements separately.
`Total Revenue =  Ticket Revenue + Food Revenue + Advertisement Revenue`

slides.headline: Assumptions

**Screens Estimate:**

Tier-2 cities: `150 cities × 8 screens = 1200 screens`,
Tier-3 cities: around `100 screens`.
Total screens = `400 + 1200 + 100 = 1700 screens`.
Each screen has around `200 seats`.
Average ticket price, including different ticket tiers, is `₹350` in Tier-1 and `₹250` in Tier-2/3.
Occupancy: `25%` on weekdays and `70%` on weekends.
Around `70%` viewers buy food/snacks like popcorn, burgers, and fries worth `₹150`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:

Total revenue in a week from tickets = screens × ticket cost × number of seats filled
`(50×8×350 + 150×8×250 + 100×250) × (5×0.25 + 2×0.7) × 200`
= **24.6 Cr INR**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Advertising and Rental Revenue:**
Assumptions:
• A movie lasts for one week in the theatre.
• Average money generated at the box office by one film: `150 Cr`
• Revenue shared by PVR: `10%`
Total: `0.1 × 150 = 15 Cr INR`

**Step 4: Total:**
`24.6 + 9.5 + 15 = 49.1 Cr INR/week`
≈ **49 Cr INR/week**

revisionCards.title: Amazon Product Searches in India per Minute
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Calculate the number of Amazon product searches in India in a minute.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine Amazon searches as people browsing in a huge online mall. Shopping increases during festivals and weddings, so we estimate searches for each period and average them.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We are estimating Amazon product searches in India per minute.
2. Only searches made on the Amazon app are considered.
3. Searching the same product again is counted as another search.
4. We estimate searches month-wise for a year and then take the average.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Categorization**:
Instead of directly guessing searches per minute, we first estimate the number of Amazon users in India. Then we divide the year into festive season, wedding season, and rest of the year because shopping behavior changes across these periods.
`Average Searches/minute = Yearly Weighted Searches ÷ 12 months`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**User Base Estimate:**
India’s population is assumed to be around `150 Cr`.
People with internet access = `60%`, giving `90 Cr` internet users.
Online shopping users = `80%` of internet users.
Amazon market share is assumed to be `40%`.
Total Amazon users = `150 × 0.6 × 0.8 × 0.4 = 28.8 Cr`.
Age split: `0–18 years = 10%`, `18–50 years = 70%`, `50+ years = 20%`.
Market time split: festivals = `4 months`, wedding season = `2 months`, rest of year = `6 months`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Festive Season Searches:**
For `0–18 years`, most users mainly browse, so only `60%` are active shoppers with `0.25 search/day`, while `40%` search around `0.5/day`.
For `18–50 years`, earning users, so `70%` are heavy shoppers with `1 search/day`, while `30%` do casual searches with `0.5/day`.
For `50+ years`, users mostly compare prices, so `0.5 search/day`.
Total = `28.8 × 0.5 × (0.10×0.60×0.25 + 0.10×0.40×0.50 + 0.70×0.70×1 + 0.70×0.30×0.5 + 0.20×0.5)`
= **10.51 Cr searches/day ≈ 73000 searches/minute**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 2: Wedding Season Searches:**
For `0–18 years`, purchase intent is low, so we assume `1 search/day` mainly due to interest.
For `18–50 years`, shopping is highest because they buy clothes, gifts, and household items, so we take `2 searches/day` for buying, `1` for comparison, and `0.5` for browsing.
For `50+ years`, activity is moderate, so we assume `2 searches/day` for comparison and shopping.
Total = `28.8 × 0.3 × (0.10×1×1 + 0.70×1×(2 + 1 + 0.5) + 0.20×1×2)`
= **25.48 Cr searches/day ≈ 177000 searches/minute**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Rest of the Year Searches:**
For `0–18 years`, activity is mostly casual browsing, so we assume `0.25 search/day`.
For `18–50 years`, users continue regular browsing and comparison, so we assume `0.25 search/day`.
For `50+ years`, online shopping activity is very low, so we take it as negligible.
Only `5%` users are assumed to shop daily during this period.
Total = `28.8 × 0.05 × (0.10×1×0.25 + 0.70×1×0.25 + 0)`
= **5.76 Cr searches/day ≈ 2000 searches/minute**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 4: Final Average:**
Festive season = `4 months`, Wedding season = `2 months`, Rest of year = `6 months`
Average searches/minute = `(73000×4 + 177000×2 + 2000×6) ÷ 12`
= **54800 searches/minute**

Assuming an arbitrary number such as 500 pizzas per day without considering customer traffic patterns.
